name: Design a Chaos Engineering Platform
intent: Let teams break small parts of production on purpose, to test a stated hypothesis about steady state, with limits on how much can break and an automatic stop the moment a guardrail is crossed.
codeTitle: a chaos experiment runner with blast-radius and abort guardrails
finalIntro: One experiment, from hypothesis to report, and one that is stopped by its guardrail.
prompt: Design a platform that lets engineering teams run chaos experiments on a production fleet of thousands of instances. Teams state a steady-state hypothesis, inject faults such as latency, errors, killed processes and network partitions, and learn whether the system holds. The platform must keep customers safe, stop by itself when things go wrong, schedule game days and report what was found.
functional: Define an experiment as a steady-state hypothesis plus a fault, a target and a duration
Inject latency, errors, process kills and network partitions
Limit the blast radius by percentage, by cell or zone, and by service
Abort automatically and roll the fault back when a guardrail metric is breached
Schedule game days and recurring small experiments, with owners and approvals
Report the timeline, the verdict on the hypothesis and the follow-up actions
nonFunctional: Every fault is reversible, and is removed within 10 seconds of an abort
A guardrail breach is detected within about 10 seconds, even if the control plane is down
A failure of the chaos platform itself must never leave a fault behind
Thousands of instances and hundreds of experiments per month
Experiments never run during an incident, a deploy freeze or when the error budget is spent
Every start, abort and result is audited

firstAttempt.text: An engineer logs in to a few production servers and kills processes or adds network delay by hand, while watching a dashboard. Nobody wrote down what was expected, and the experiment ends when the engineer decides it should.
limits: There is no hypothesis, so nobody can say what counts as passing or failing
Nothing limits how much breaks, and one wrong command can take down a whole service
If the engineer looks away or loses their connection, the fault stays in place
Nothing is recorded, so results cannot be repeated or compared
It happens whenever someone feels like it, including during a real incident

steps.title: State the hypothesis in measurable terms
steps.problem: Breaking things without saying what should happen teaches nothing, because nobody can tell a pass from a fail, or a real problem from normal noise.
steps.fix: Every experiment is a record in the experiment store, created through the API. It names a steady-state metric taken from the service's golden signals, such as the checkout success rate or the 99th percentile latency, the baseline measured over the previous hour, and the hypothesis: 'with two of ten instances returning errors, the success rate stays above 95%'. The platform reads the metrics system to compute the baseline, and refuses to start if the baseline is already unhealthy.
steps.tradeoff: Results become a clear yes or no, and repeatable. Choosing a good steady-state metric takes real thought, a noisy metric gives false verdicts, and a hypothesis that is too loose passes everything.

steps.title: Inject faults through agents that can always undo them
steps.problem: Real failures come in a few shapes: slow responses, errors, dead processes and cut networks. Each needs a safe way to be created on demand and to be removed again.
steps.fix: A fault agent runs on every host, or as a sidecar proxy next to each service. The control plane sends it a fault: add 300 ms of latency, return HTTP 500 for 30% of requests, kill the process, or drop packets to a named set of addresses to make a partition. Every fault carries a time to live, so the agent removes it by itself when the time runs out, even if the control plane never speaks to it again. Agents only accept faults signed by the control plane.
steps.tradeoff: The four kinds of failure cover most real outages, and the time to live means a lost connection cannot leave a fault behind. Agents have privileges that could do harm, so they need strong authentication, and a fault injected in a proxy is only an approximation of a real failure deep in the network.

steps.title: Limit the blast radius before anything starts
steps.problem: An experiment that is allowed to touch everything is just an outage with a good name.
steps.fix: Before it starts, a planner checks the request against limits: at most a set percentage of a service's instances, at most one cell or zone, and a list of services that are never targeted. It also checks the world around: no open incident, no deploy in progress, enough error budget left. The experiment then ramps up in stages, for example 1%, 5% and 20% of the allowed targets, and each stage must stay healthy before the next begins. The first run of a new experiment always uses a tiny slice.
steps.tradeoff: A mistake can only hurt a small part of the fleet, and teams gain confidence step by step. Small slices may not reveal problems that only appear at scale, so the limits are raised gradually as trust grows, and some tests of whole-region failure need a dedicated event.

steps.title: Abort automatically when a guardrail is breached
steps.problem: A person watching a dashboard reacts in minutes, but a bad experiment can hurt customers in seconds, and the person may not be watching at all.
steps.fix: A watchdog reads the guardrail metrics every few seconds, for example the success rate of the whole service, which must stay above 90% even though the hypothesis allows 95% in the target slice. A breach, or a missing reading, makes it send an abort to every agent, which removes the faults and reports back. The watchdog runs as a separate service from the control plane, so it works even if the API is down. If agents stop hearing from it, their time to live ends the fault anyway.
steps.tradeoff: Customers see at most a few seconds of impact, and abort needs no human. A too-sensitive guardrail aborts on ordinary noise and teams learn nothing, a too-loose one hurts users first, and treating missing data as a breach will sometimes abort a healthy experiment.

steps.title: Schedule game days and keep small experiments running
steps.problem: Experiments run once and forgotten prove nothing about next month's code, and big team exercises need preparation and people.
steps.fix: A scheduler holds two kinds of runs. Game days are booked on a calendar with an owner, a list of attendees, an approval from the service's on-call, and a notification in the team channel before and after. Recurring experiments, such as 'kill one instance of each stateless service every weekday morning', run on their own during working hours, when people are present to respond. Freeze windows, holidays and busy periods block all runs.
steps.tradeoff: People are ready when something unexpected happens, and regressions are caught continuously. Approvals add friction, and experiments in working hours are only safe because the blast radius and the abort are already in place.

steps.title: Report the verdict and follow the findings
steps.problem: If the learning stays in the heads of those who attended, the same weakness is found again next year.
steps.fix: When an experiment ends, or aborts, the platform assembles a report from the store: the hypothesis, the faults with their exact start and stop times, the metric graphs with the fault window marked, the verdict (held, disproved or aborted) and a link to traces of the failed requests. Findings become tickets owned by the team, and a dashboard tracks which services have been tested, which hypotheses failed and how long fixes take.
steps.tradeoff: Each experiment leaves evidence, and resilience becomes something that can be measured over time. Reports need curation to stay useful, and counting the experiments run rewards the wrong behaviour if it is not tied to fixes.

failures.scenario: The metrics pipeline goes blind during an experiment
failures.impact: The watchdog cannot see the guardrail, so a harmful fault could run unnoticed.
failures.answer: Missing data counts as a breach, so the watchdog aborts and the experiment is marked inconclusive. Independently, every fault has a short time to live that the control plane must renew while readings are healthy, so a blind platform loses its faults within seconds.

failures.scenario: A fault agent crashes while a fault is active
failures.impact: A rule that drops packets or delays requests could stay on the host with no one to remove it.
failures.answer: Faults are installed so they expire by themselves: a rule carries a deadline, and the host cleans up expired rules at start-up. A supervisor restarts the agent, which first removes every fault it cannot match to a live experiment. A periodic audit compares the faults on hosts with the experiments in the store and raises an alert for any stray.

failures.scenario: Retries turn a small fault into a wider outage
failures.impact: Two failing instances cause clients to retry, and the extra load pushes the healthy instances past their capacity, so the damage is far larger than the planned slice.
failures.answer: The guardrail watches the whole service, not only the target slice, so the spread is caught and the experiment aborts. The finding itself is valuable: it shows missing retry limits or too little headroom, and the report links to the traces that show the amplification.

failures.scenario: An experiment passes only because the metric is too noisy to show harm
failures.impact: The team believes the system is resilient, but a real failure later proves otherwise.
failures.answer: Each experiment compares the fault window with a control group of untouched instances and with the baseline, and requires enough requests in the window for a meaningful result. A result with too little traffic is reported as inconclusive, not as a pass, and the hypothesis is tightened.

alternatives.title: Where faults are injected

options.name: In the application with a library
options.pro: Precise: it can fail one particular call
options.con: Every language needs a library, and the test code ships with the product

options.name: In a sidecar or proxy
options.pro: Works for any language, and easy to turn on and off
options.con: Cannot imitate a dying process or a full disk

options.name: On the host or cloud, with a node agent or provider API
options.pro: Real failures: kills, packet loss, whole zones
options.con: Broad privileges and a bigger blast if misused

alternatives.pick: A sidecar for latency and errors, and a signed host agent for kills and partitions.

alternatives.title: Where experiments run

options.name: Only in staging
options.con: Different traffic, data and scale, so it misses real weaknesses

options.name: In production, with limits and automatic abort
options.con: Needs the safety machinery and organizational trust

alternatives.pick: Start in staging to debug the experiment, then production with a tiny blast radius.

alternatives.title: When experiments happen

options.name: Occasional game days
options.pro: Whole-team learning and room for big scenarios

options.name: Continuous small experiments
options.pro: Catches regressions soon after they are shipped
options.con: Less dramatic, and needs the automation to be trusted

alternatives.pick: Both: continuous small experiments, and a quarterly game day for large scenarios.

alternatives.title: Who stops a bad experiment

options.name: A person with a stop button
An automatic watchdog
options.con: Needs well-chosen thresholds, and can abort on noise

alternatives.pick: Automatic abort as the main protection, with a manual stop button as well.

roles.label: Engineers
roles.description: Teams that write and review experiments.

roles.label: Control plane
roles.description: The API that accepts, validates and starts experiments.

roles.label: Safety and faults
roles.description: The planner, fault agents, target services and the abort watchdog.

quiz.question: An engineer SSHs into 3 production hosts, adds 300 ms of network delay by hand and watches a dashboard. Halfway through, their laptop loses its connection, and the delay stays on the hosts for hours. Which platform design prevents this?
options: A nightly job that reboots every host touched by an experiment during the day, so that leftover faults are gone by the morning
A fault agent on every host that gives each fault a time to live and removes it itself when that expires
An email reminder sent to the engineer when an experiment has run for more than 15 minutes, with a link to the undo script
A rule that a second engineer must also watch the dashboard and run the undo command by hand
quiz.explanation: A time to live makes the fault remove itself, so a lost connection or a crashed platform cannot leave it behind. Reminders, nightly reboots and a second human all depend on someone acting, and the damage continues until they do.

quiz.question: An experiment makes 2 of 10 instances of a service return errors. The hypothesis only concerns the target instances. Clients retry failed calls, and the extra load pushes the 8 healthy instances past their capacity, so the whole service slows down. The watchdog reads only the target instances' metrics. What change lets the platform stop this in time?
options: Guard the success rate of the whole service, with a looser threshold such as 90%, checked every few seconds
Run the experiment on a single instance instead, so that the retries cannot overload the healthy ones and hide the real behaviour
Read the target instances' metrics every second instead of every 10 seconds, so that the abort comes as early as possible
Tighten the hypothesis so that the target instances must keep a 99% success rate while the fault is active and the run ends
quiz.explanation: The harm is on instances the watchdog does not look at, so the guardrail must watch the whole service. Reading the wrong metric faster, or tightening the hypothesis, still misses the spread. One instance may hide the retry effect rather than prevent it.

quiz.question: During a 20-minute experiment that adds 300 ms of latency to 5% of the instances, the metrics pipeline stops delivering data for 40 seconds. The control plane that renews fault leases is healthy. What should the platform do?
options: Keep the fault running and wait, because missing data is not evidence of harm and an abort would waste the whole experiment
Reuse the last good reading as the current value until real data returns, so that the experiment is not disturbed at all
Abort and remove the faults, mark the experiment inconclusive, and renew fault leases only while a healthy reading arrives
Extend every fault's time to live by 60 seconds so that the pipeline has time to recover before any decision is made
quiz.explanation: Without readings nobody can tell whether customers are being hurt, so missing data counts as a breach and the fault must go. The cost is an occasional abort of a healthy run. Reusing the last reading or extending the lease keeps a fault active while the platform is blind.
